newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans urged not to put end to Holocaust debate.
newsitem.headline: Germans urged not to put end to Holocaust debate.

text.p: Klaus von Dohnanyi, the son of a German anti-Nazi resistance fighter, urged his compatriots on Monday not to put an end to the debate on German guilt for the Nazis' attempt to wipe out Europe's Jews.

On the 52nd anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz death camp, being marked this year for the second time as a day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust, Dohnanyi dismissed suggestions that Germans had shown enough remorse for the past.

"Putting an end to the debate about the Nazi era would only backfire on us. It would prevent us from understanding and explaining the causes and realities of Nazism," he told the lower house of parliament in a ceremonial address.

Dohnanyi, a former mayor of Hamburg, said it was essential for younger generations born long after the Holocaust to condemn the Nazis and feel shame for what they did, because otherwise the rest of the world might think Germany had not changed.
"Sometimes the Nazi past is used as a cheap judgement against democratic Germany," said Dohnanyi, speaking 52 years to the day after Auschwitz was liberated.
"Just as we have prejudices about Turks and Poles so, given our Nazi past, we shouldn't be surprised if some people outside Germany say the Germans have not changed," he said.
Dohnanyi criticised the design of a Holocaust memorial, planned for central Berlin, which has been criticised by politicians, media and Holocaust survivors.
The design envisages a tombstone-shaped memorial the size of a football pitch inscribed with the names of millions of European Jews who died in the Holocaust.

He said Germans should not reduce the atrocities committed by the Nazis to listing numbers of victims and perpetrators names, but commemorate the Holocaust by considering the victims' plight on a more human scale.

"It has to be more than just counting the victims and carving this in stone. It has to touch and shake us. It must move us to get a sense of the (victims') suffering and fate just as the Anne Frank museum does in Amsterdam," he said.

Anne Frank kept a diary of the time she and her Jewish family spent sheltering from the Nazis in Amsterdam. She was eventually discovered and deported, and died aged 15 in Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in northern Germany.

The day of remembrance was marked for the first time last year, following a proposal by President Roman Herzog. The day is not a public holiday but is marked by schools, local authorities, associations and church groups.
Dohnanyi's father, Hans, engaged in resistance activity while working for Hitler's defence chief Admiral Wilhelm Canaris and was murdered in a concentration camp in 1945.
